**https://www.cnn.com/2023/07/25/health/weight-loss-diabetes-drugs-gastroparesis/index.html**    **Facial lipoatrophy with semaglutide-related weight loss**February 10, 2023  **https://www.mdedge.com/dermatology/article/261159/aesthetic-dermatology/facial-lipoatrophy-semaglutide-related-weight-loss**    ---------------------------------------Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonists are medications approved for treatment of diabetes that recently have also been used off label for weight loss.1 Studies have found increased risks of gastrointestinal adverse events (biliary disease,2 pancreatitis,3 bowel obstruction,4 and gastroparesis5) in patients with diabetes.2-5 Because such patients have higher baseline risk for gastrointestinal adverse events, risk in patients taking these drugs for other indications may differ. Randomized trials examining efficacy of GLP-1 agonists for weight loss were not designed to capture these events2 due to small sample sizes and short follow-up. We examined gastrointestinal adverse events associated with GLP-1 agonists used for weight loss in a clinical setting. **Results** Our cohort included 4144 liraglutide, 613 semaglutide, and 654 bupropion-naltrexone users. Incidence rates for the 4 outcomes were elevated among GLP-1 agonists compared with bupropion-naltrexone users (Table 1). For example, incidence of biliary disease (per 1000 person-years) was 11.7 for semaglutide, 18.6 for liraglutide, and 12.6 for bupropion-naltrexone and 4.6, 7.9, and 1.0, respectively, for pancreatitis. Use of GLP-1 agonists compared with bupropion-naltrexone was associated with increased risk of pancreatitis (adjusted HR, 9.09 [95% CI, 1.25-66.00]), bowel obstruction (HR, 4.22 [95% CI, 1.02-17.40]), and gastroparesis (HR, 3.67 [95% CI, 1.15-11.90) but not biliary disease (HR, 1.50 [

]), and gastroparesis (HR, 3.67 [95% CI, 1.15-11.90) but not biliary disease (HR, 1.50 [95% CI, 0.89-2.53]). Exclusion of hyperlipidemia from the analysis did not change the results (Table 2). Inclusion of GLP-1 agonists regardless of history of obesity reduced HRs and narrowed CIs but did not change the significance of the results (Table 2). E-value HRs did not suggest potential confounding by BMI. **Discussion** This study found that use of GLP-1 agonists for weight loss compared with use of bupropion-naltrexone was associated with increased risk of pancreatitis, gastroparesis, and bowel obstruction but not biliary disease. Given the wide use of these drugs, these adverse events, although rare, must be considered by patients who are contemplating using the drugs for weight loss because the risk-benefit calculus for this group might differ from that of those who use them for diabetes. Limitations include that although all GLP-1 agonist users had a record for obesity without diabetes, whether GLP-1 agonists were all used for weight loss is uncertain. |  |

## Study Design

- Randomized
- International multicenter
- Double-blind
- Placebo-controlled

Patients with overweight or obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥27 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) and established CVD were randomized to receive once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (n = 8,803) vs. placebo (n = 8,801). Semaglutide was initiated at 0.24 mg once weekly and increased every 4 weeks as tolerated until the target (2.4 mg weekly) or maximally tolerated dose was reached. Management of incident DM during the trial was deferred to the treating provider, although open-label use of a GLP-1 RA was prohibited.

- Total number of enrollees: 17,604
- Mean duration of follow-up: 40 months
- Mean patient age: 62 years
- Percentage female: 28%

Inclusion criteria:

- Age ≥45 years
- BMI ≥27 kg/m<sup>2</sup>
- Prior myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, or peripheral arterial disease with claudication and ankle-brachial index <0.85, prior revascularization, or amputation

Exclusion criteria:

- MI, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischemic attack ≤60 days prior
- Upcoming planned revascularization
- New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV heart failure (HF) symptoms
- History of DM or hemoglobin A<sub>1c</sub> (HbA<sub>1c</sub> ) ≥6.5%
- GLP-1 RA use ≤90 days prior
- Acute pancreatitis ≤180 days prior
- Chronic pancreatitis
- Personal or first-degree relative history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 or medullary thyroid carcinoma
- End-stage renal disease or dialysis requirement

Limitations of the trial include the small number of Black patients, a lack of data regarding biomarkers of alcohol consumption, genetic polymorphisms as a determinant of therapeutic response, and changes in body composition during therapy. Also, given the small number of lean patients, definitive conclusions of benefit in this population cannot be made.

#### **Trial Procedures and Outcomes** 

Patients were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio by means of a centralized system to receive onceweekly subcutaneous semaglutide (at a dose of 2.4 mg) or placebo in addition to standard care for MASH and related coexisting illnesses (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). Lifestyle counseling and management of coexisting conditions were recommended in alignment with guidelines.<sup>19,20</sup> Randomization was stratified according to the presence or absence of type 2 diabetes at screening, fibrosis stage (2 or 3), and region (Japan, East Asia [excluding Japan], or the rest of the world). Semaglutide and placebo solutions were provided in prefilled pen injectors. 

The starting dose of semaglutide was 0.25 mg once weekly, which was increased every 4 weeks to once-weekly doses of 0.5 mg, 1.0 mg, 1.7 mg, and 2.4 mg until the target dose of 2.4 mg was reached after the 16-week dose-escalation period. Patients could continue receiving a lower dose if they had unacceptable side effects while receiving the designated target dose but were recommended to make at least one attempt to re-escalate to the designated target dose of 2.4 mg once weekly, per the investigator’s discretion. Additional details regarding the semaglutide dose selection are provided in the Supplementary Appendix. Semaglutide or placebo was discontinued in case of current or planned pregnancy, suspicion of acute pancreatitis, abnormal liver-enzyme values indicating drug-induced liver injury, or a diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma. 

Two liver biopsies, with centrally read results, were required to make the assessment of the primary end points for part 1: one biopsy performed during the screening period (or the pre-

Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes<sup>7</sup> and overweight or obesity,<sup>8</sup> with reports of improvements in cardiovascular and renal outcomes in these populations.<sup>9-11</sup> In a previous phase 2 trial, the effects of once-daily subcutaneous semaglutide (at doses of 0.1 mg, 0.2 mg, or 0.4 mg) as compared with placebo were investigated in patients with biopsy-defined MASH and liver fibrosis (stages 1, 2, and 3) during a 72-week period.<sup>12</sup> A significantly higher percentage of patients who received semaglutide at a dose of 0.4 mg than those who received placebo had resolution of steatohepatitis with no worsening of fibrosis (59% vs. 17%, P<0.001). In addition, patients in the semaglutide group had a reduction in fibrosis stage, although the improvement was not statistically significant. 

Currently, only resmetirom has accelerated approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of MASH with stage 2 or 3 liver fibrosis,<sup>13,14</sup> with studies ongoing to establish the clinical benefits for full approval. Thus, there is an unmet need for additional treatment options. Moreover, given that patients with MASH are at high risk for adverse liver outcomes and cardiovascular disease, treatments should ideally address both conditions.<sup>15,16</sup> Here, we report interim efficacy results from the first 800 patients who completed 72 weeks of treatment in the ESSENCE trial evaluating once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (at a dose of 2.4 mg) as compared with placebo in patients with biopsy-defined MASH and fibrosis stage 2 or 3.<sup>17</sup> Safety reporting is based on all data that were available at the time of the datacutoff date.

### Results 

#### **Patient Characteristics** 

From May 27, 2021, to April 18, 2023, a total of 1197 patients underwent randomization. Of these patients, 1195 were included in the overall safety population. Reported here are data for the first 800 patients who were enrolled in the trial, including 534 patients who were assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide at a dose of 2.4 mg and 266 patients who were assigned to receive placebo. 

Baseline characteristics were generally similar in the two trial groups (Table 1 and Table S2 and Fig. S3). The mean (±SD) age of the total population was 56.0±11.6, and the mean bodymass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) was 34.6±7.2. Most patients were White (67.5%) and female (57.1%), and 55.9% of the patients had type 2 diabetes; 250 patients (31.3%) had stage 2 fibrosis, and 550 (68.8%) had stage 3 fibrosis. The percentages of patients according to geographic location were as follows: Asia (25.1%), Europe (25.3%), North America (35.0%), and South America (7.9%); the location for the remaining 6.8% of patients was listed as “other.” The representativeness of the trial patients is detailed in Table S3.

# Semaglutide Effects on Cardiovascular Outcomes in People With Overweight or Obesity - SELECT

## Contribution To Literature:

Highlighted text has been updated as of September 12, 2024.

The SELECT trial showed that in patients with overweight or obesity and established CVD but without diabetes, once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide was associated with a decreased risk of MACE comprised of CV death, nonfatal MI, and stroke compared with placebo.

## Description:

The goal of the trial was to determine the association of subcutaneous semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), with cardiovascular (CV) events in a secondary prevention cohort of patients with overweight or obesity and prior CV disease (CVD) without diabetes mellitus (DM).

Patients with MASH frequently have cardiometabolic coexisting illnesses.<sup>32,33</sup> In our trial, 55.9% of the patients had type 2 diabetes, and 

72.8% had obesity. As in previous studies, semaglutide improved multiple cardiometabolic features, including glycemic control and weight loss, as well as insulin resistance.<sup>10,11,34-36</sup> These findings are important because metabolic dysfunction is an upstream event driving hepatic lipotoxicity and, subsequently, steatohepatitis and fibrogenesis. Thus, semaglutide treatment addressed the primary pathogenic driver of MASH.<sup>37,38</sup> The drug also provided a holistic therapeutic approach to both liver disease and associated cardiometabolic illnesses.<sup>37</sup> Although semaglutide can be safely used in patients with cirrhosis,<sup>39</sup> its efficacy in this population has not been established. It is therefore essential that patients with MASH be screened for cirrhosis and treated accordingly.<sup>40,41</sup> 

With the dose-escalation approach used in our trial, which mirrors the approach used in clinical practice, 89.3% of the patients continued to receive semaglutide at one of the prescribed doses by week 72. No new safety signals emerged, and the safety profile was consistent with the body of evidence for semaglutide,<sup>12,42</sup>

#### **Secondary End Points** 

Both resolution of steatohepatitis and fibrosis reduction occurred in 32.7% of the patients in the semaglutide group and in 16.1% of those in the placebo group (estimated difference, 16.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 10.2 to 22.8; P<0.001) (Fig. S7). The mean percentage change in body weight from baseline at week 72 was −10.5% with semaglutide and −2.0% with placebo (estimated difference, −8.5 percentage points; 95% CI, −9.6 to −7.4; P<0.001). The mean change from baseline at week 72 for the bodily pain score on 

the SF-36 was 0.9 in the semaglutide group and −0.5 in the placebo group, indicating less pain with semaglutide (estimated difference, 1.3; 95% CI, 0.0 to 2.7; P = 0.05), a finding that did not meet the prespecified criteria for statistical significance (P<0.0045). 

The results of noninvasive testing — including for the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) score, liver stiffness (as assessed by vibration-controlled transient elastography) (Fig. 2), FibroScan-AST (FAST) score, N-terminal propeptide of type III collagen (PRO-C3) level (Table S6), and γ-glutamyltransferase level (Fig. S8 and Table S6) — appeared to be better with semaglutide than with placebo after 72 weeks, with a decline in the aminotransferase levels already apparent at 12 weeks (Fig. S9). The percentage of patients who met the prespecified definition of a decrease in the ELF score of 0.5 or more was 55.8% in the semaglutide group and 25.5% in the placebo group. The percentage of patients who met the response criteria for a decrease in liver stiffness of 30% or more was 52.0% with semaglutide and 30.3% with placebo (Fig. S10 and S11).

#### **Patients** 

Eligible adults (≥18 years of age) had histologically documented steatohepatitis and liver fibrosis of stage 2 or 3, according to the Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis Clinical Research Network (NASH CRN) classification,<sup>18</sup> and a nonalcoholic fatty liver disease activity score (NAS) of 4 or more. (The NAS is a composite score of steatosis, lobular inflammation, and hepatocyte ballooning, with a score of ≥1 in each component, all based on an evaluation by a central pathologist. The scores range from 0 to 8, with a score of 5 or more indicating a diagnosis of definite NASH and a score of 3 or less ruling it out.<sup>18</sup> ) 

Key exclusion criteria were chronic liver disease other than MASLD; an average alcohol consumption of more than 20 g per day for women and more than 30 g per day for men; hepatic decompensation or a Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score of more than 12 points at screening; an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) or alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level of more than 5 times the upper limit of the normal range at screening; an estimated glomerular filtration rate of less than 30 ml per minute per 1.73 m<sup>2</sup> of body-

After the exclusion of insulin use, semaglutide reduced insulin resistance slightly more among the patients who had type 2 diabetes than among those without type 2 diabetes (Table S8). More patients receiving semaglutide appeared to have reductions in steatosis, ballooning, and total NAS (Fig. S12). Patients with fibrosis stage 2 appeared to have less fibrosis progression at week 72 with semaglutide than with placebo (Fig. S13). Results regarding patients with fibrosis stage 3 and progression to cirrhosis are not reported here because these events are prespecified to be reported in part 2 of the trial. 

#### **Safety** 

A total of 83.5% of the patients in the semaglutide group maintained the target dose of 2.4 mg until week 72. The percentage of patients who had a reported adverse event was 86.3% with semaglutide and 79.7% with placebo; 13.4% of the patients in each group had a serious adverse event. Adverse events leading to premature trial discontinuation occurred in 2.6% of the patients in the semaglutide group and in 3.3% of those in the placebo group (Table 3). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal disorders in both groups. Nausea, diarrhea, constipation, and vomiting were more common in the semaglutide group. The incidence of acute pancreatitis was similar in the two groups. Nine patients died (three in the semaglutide group and six in the placebo group), with no evident clustering of cause of death. Additional safety data are presented in Tables S9 through S13.

## Principal Findings:

The primary outcome, major adverse CV events (MACE: composite of CV death, nonfatal MI, and nonfatal stroke), for semaglutide vs. placebo, was: 6.5% vs. 8.0% (hazard ratio [HR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72-0.90, p < 0.001).

Prespecified subgroup analyses of the primary outcome for semaglutide vs. placebo:

- Female vs. male: HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.66-1.07) vs. HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.70-0.90)
- HbA<sub>1c</sub> <5.7% vs. ≥5.7%: HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.68-1.00) vs. HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69-0.90)
- HF vs. no HF: HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.60-0.87) vs. HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.74-0.97), p for interaction = 0.19
- HFrEF vs. HFpEF: HR 0.65 (95% CI 0.49-0.87) vs. HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.51-0.91), p for interaction = 0.82

Secondary outcomes for semaglutide vs. placebo:

- CV death: 2.5% vs. 3.0% (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.71-1.01, p = 0.07)
- All-cause death: 4.3% vs. 5.2% (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.71-0.93)
- Nonfatal MI: 2.7% vs. 3.7% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.61-0.85)

HF composite outcome, CV death or HF hospitalization, for semaglutide vs. placebo: 3.4% vs. 4.1% (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71-0.96)
